A song is a conversation. The singer says a line and then stops to breathe, and in that gap the band
answers. The answer is a **fill**: a short figure from the piano, the bass, the guitar or the drums that
fills the space before the next line. A **riff** is different: a short figure the band repeats again and
again under the song, so it becomes the song's signature. A **lick** is a player's stock phrase, the kind
of figure fills and solos are made of.

This page plays each of them on the band. Press ▶ Play, switch players in and out with the buttons beside
it, and switch the figures on and off with the second row of buttons. The staff underneath shows what the
band will play. The tempo slider at the bottom of the page slows everything down.

::: {.callout-note}
## MYP4: Rock and the Pop Ballads
Our statement of inquiry is *Art allows us to express our feelings and communicate our philosophies and
ways of life effectively.* A fill is communication inside the song: the band replying to the singer,
agreeing, pushing or comforting. For Criterion B, the fills you try (and the ones you leave out) are
practical exploration: record two versions of a phrase end, and say in your journal which one serves the
words better and why.
:::

## 1. Riff, fill, lick: three words

- **Riff:** a short phrase repeated exactly throughout a song ("Fill (music)"). Rock is full of guitar
  riffs that carry a whole verse. *Unverified (from memory, not yet checked against a source):* the riff
  usually sits on the home chord and is the first thing a listener can hum.
- **Fill:** "a short musical passage, riff, or rhythmic sound which helps to sustain the listener's
  attention", played in the breaks between phrases, especially at their ends, and changed each time rather
  than repeated ("Fill (music)"). Drummers play most of them, but guitar, bass, organ, piano, strings and
  horns all fill too (same source).
- **Lick:** *unverified:* a stock phrase in one player's vocabulary (a blues guitarist's turnaround, a
  gospel pianist's run), used in fills and solos.

The short version: **a riff repeats, a fill answers, a lick is what you answer with.**

## 2. The gap

A pop ballad's lines are usually four bars long, and the singer usually stops in the fourth bar. That
fourth bar is where the band speaks. Listen to the ballad first with no figures, then with them. With
figures on, the piano, then the bass, then the piano again take the fourth bar of each phrase, **one at a
time**.

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="pop" data-chart="C|G|Am|F|C|G|F|C|Am|F|C|G|C|G|F|C" data-tempo="72" data-on="bass comp drums" data-staves="comp bass" data-choice-label="Figures:" data-choices='[{"label":"Fills in turn","opts":{"figures":"pianoAnswer+bassWalkUp+pianoSus"}},{"label":"No fills","opts":{"figures":""}}]'></div>

**What to listen for.** Without fills the band is good wallpaper: steady, polite, a bit flat. With them
every fourth bar leans forward into the next line. Look at bar 4 on the staff: the right hand plays its
chord on beat 1, waits, then answers. Waiting is half of a fill.

**Taking turns.** Only one player fills at a time. If the piano, the bass and the drums all fill in the
same bar, the answers run into each other and nobody is heard: it sounds busy, not exciting. Bands agree on
whose turn it is, and the band here does the same.

## 3. Piano

Two fills every ballad pianist knows. The **answer**: the chord's notes coming down in eighth notes from
the top, octave, fifth, third, root, landing ready for the next chord. The **sus**: the chord with its
third raised to the fourth (a *sus4*) on beat 3, falling back to the third on beat 4, a sigh in the
harmony.

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="pop" data-chart="C|G|Am|F" data-tempo="72" data-on="comp" data-staves="comp" data-comp="piano" data-choice-label="Bar 4:" data-choices='[{"label":"Answer (down the chord)","opts":{"figures":"pianoAnswer"}},{"label":"Sus4 to 3","opts":{"figures":"pianoSus"}},{"label":"No fill","opts":{"figures":""}}]'></div>

**How to play it.** Left hand: keep the octave on the root ringing (pedal down). Right hand: strike the
chord on 1, lift on 2, and play the answer with fingers 5 3 2 1 (octave, fifth, third, root), each a little
softer than the one before. For the sus, move only one finger: the third steps up a half or whole step and
back.

## 4. Bass

The bass fills by **walking to the next chord**. Two ways: the **walk-up**, three quarter notes climbing
5, 6, 7 of the next chord's scale into its root; and the **approach**, two eighth notes on beat 4 a whole
step and a half step below the next root.

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="pop" data-chart="C|G|Am|F|C|G|F|C" data-tempo="72" data-on="bass drums" data-staves="bass" data-choice-label="Bar 4 and 8:" data-choices='[{"label":"Walk-up","opts":{"figures":"bassWalkUp"}},{"label":"Approach","opts":{"figures":"bassApproach"}},{"label":"No fill","opts":{"figures":""}}]'></div>

**What to look for.** The fill always ends on the note just below the next root, so it pulls into the new
bar. Into C that is B; into Am it is G♯. Practise slowly with a metronome: the fill must not rush, or the
next bar arrives early.

## 5. Guitar: the rock lick and the riff

The rock guitarist's fill is a **minor-pentatonic lick** from the chord's root: down from the octave, ♭7,
5, ♭3, then back to the chord. The rock **riff** climbs the same scale, root, ♭3, 4, 5, on beats 3 and 4 of
every second bar, after the power chord on 1. Switch between them: the riff is always there, the lick
only at the ends of phrases.

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="rock" data-chart="E|A|E|B|E|A|E|B" data-tempo="112" data-on="bass comp drums" data-staves="comp" data-comp="guitar" data-choice-label="Guitar:" data-choices='[{"label":"Lick at phrase ends","opts":{"figures":"guitarLick+bassApproach"}},{"label":"Riff every 2nd bar","opts":{"figures":"guitarRiff"}},{"label":"Riff and lick","opts":{"figures":"guitarRiff+guitarLick+bassApproach"}},{"label":"Strumming only","opts":{"figures":""}}]'></div>

**How to play it.** In E, every note of the lick is in the open position: E (open top string), D (B string,
3rd fret), B (open B), G (open G). The riff is low: E (open low string), G (3rd fret), A (open A), B (A
string, 2nd fret). Mute the strings you are not playing with the side of the picking
hand. *Unverified:* a bend on the ♭3 (a quarter-tone towards the major third) is the classic blues-rock
touch; the band here plays it straight.

## 6. Famous riffs, intros and outros

Short excerpts of riffs everyone knows, for study in class. These are **read from notation**: each is the
music example printed on that song's Wikipedia page (English, German or Italian), converted note for note
for the band; the page is named in the Works Cited. They are excerpts as Wikipedia gives them, not full
transcriptions, and the octave the guitar and bass sound in is the site's reading (guitar and bass music is
written an octave above where it sounds). Many songs **start** with their riff alone (the intro) and
**end** with it, or with a tag (the outro): switch every player but one off to hear the riff as an intro.

### Guitar

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="rock" data-chart="E|E|E|E" data-tempo="132" data-on="comp drums" data-staves="comp" data-comp="guitar" data-choice-label="Riff:" data-choices='[{"label":"(I Can’t Get No) Satisfaction (The Rolling Stones (1965))","opts":{"figures":"satisfaction"},"chart":"E|E|E|E"},{"label":"Day Tripper (The Beatles (1965))","opts":{"figures":"dayTripper"},"chart":"E|E|E|E"},{"label":"Johnny B. Goode (intro) (Chuck Berry (1958))","opts":{"figures":"johnnyB"},"chart":"Bb|Bb|Bb|Bb|Bb"},{"label":"Black Sabbath (Black Sabbath (1970))","opts":{"figures":"blackSabbath"},"chart":"G|G|G|G"},{"label":"Layla (Derek and the Dominos (1970))","opts":{"figures":"layla"},"chart":"Dm|Dm|Dm|Dm|Dm"},{"label":"Stairway to Heaven (intro) (Led Zeppelin (1971))","opts":{"figures":"stairway"},"chart":"Am|Am|Am|Am"}]'></div>

- *Satisfaction*: three notes, B, C♯, D, and the space between them; the riff is mostly rhythm.
- *Day Tripper*: the E chord's own notes (E, G♯, B) with the blues ♭3 (G) and ♭7 (D) slipped in.
- *Johnny B. Goode*: the intro, double stops (two strings at once) hammered in eighths, then a run down.
- *Black Sabbath*: G, the G an octave up, then C♯: the **tritone**, the interval three whole tones wide,
  slow and heavy. A feeling made from one interval.
- *Layla*: a fast sixteenth-note pickup that lands on a long held D, then the same an octave up.
- *Stairway to Heaven*: the intro, a picked line over a bass that falls by half steps (A, G♯, G, F♯, F).

### Bass

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="rock" data-chart="Em|Em|Em|Em" data-tempo="110" data-on="bass drums" data-staves="bass" data-choice-label="Riff:" data-choices='[{"label":"Another One Bites the Dust (Queen (1980))","opts":{"figures":"biteDust"},"chart":"Em|Em|Em|Em"},{"label":"Stand by Me (Ben E. King (1961))","opts":{"figures":"standByMe"},"chart":"A|A|F#m|F#m|D|E|A|A"}]'></div>

- *Another One Bites the Dust*: three repeated Es, a gap, then the answer; the pickup at the end leads back.
- *Stand by Me*: one figure moved through the chords (A, F♯m, D, E): the whole song's harmony in the bass.

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="rock" data-chart="Gm|Gm|Gm|Gm" data-meter="5/4" data-tempo="150" data-on="bass drums" data-staves="bass" data-choice-label="Riff:" data-choices='[{"label":"Theme from Mission: Impossible (Lalo Schifrin (1966))","opts":{"figures":"missionBass"},"chart":"Gm|Gm|Gm|Gm"}]'></div>

*Mission: Impossible* is in **5/4**: count 1-2-3, 1-2-3, 1-2, 1-2 (eighth notes 3 + 3 + 2 + 2).

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="rock" data-chart="Bm|Bm|Bm|Bm" data-meter="7/4" data-tempo="120" data-on="bass drums" data-staves="bass" data-choice-label="Riff:" data-choices='[{"label":"Money (Pink Floyd (1973))","opts":{"figures":"money"},"chart":"Bm|Bm|Bm|Bm"}]'></div>

*Money* is in **7/4**: seven beats to a bar, the riff's notes on the beats with one triplet.

### Keys

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="pop" data-chart="Gm|Gm|Gm|Gm|Gm|Gm" data-tempo="120" data-on="comp" data-staves="comp" data-comp="piano" data-choice-label="Riff:" data-choices='[{"label":"Ashes to Ashes (hook) (David Bowie (1980))","opts":{"figures":"ashes"},"chart":"Gm|Gm|Gm|Gm|Gm|Gm"},{"label":"Shave and a Haircut (the ending tag) (traditional)","opts":{"figures":"shave"},"chart":"C|C|C|C"}]'></div>

- *Ashes to Ashes*: a three-bar hook on the synthesizer, here on the piano.
- *Shave and a Haircut*: the five-note tag and its two-note answer ("two bits"), a ready-made **outro**:
  a band can end a song with it.

**Ask yourself (Criterion A):** why does a riff become the thing everyone remembers about a song? Pick two
from this section: what does each say about the feeling of its song before a word is sung?

## 7. Drums

The drummer's fill tells the band where the phrase ends and how big the next section will be. A small
fill (a snare note or two) says "next line"; a bigger one down the toms says "here comes the chorus".
The band's drummer already does this (Fills: none, at sections only, or as usual).

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="rock" data-chart="E|A|E|B|E|A|E|B" data-tempo="112" data-on="bass comp drums" data-staves="drums" data-choice-label="Drum fills:" data-choices='[{"label":"As usual","opts":{"figures":"","fills":"auto"}},{"label":"More","opts":{"figures":"","fills":"busy"}},{"label":"None","opts":{"figures":"","fills":"none"}}]'></div>

**In a ballad** the drummer fills least of all, and often only into the chorus. A fill under the singer's
line covers the words.

## 8. The producer's view: making room

In a recording studio the question is not "can I fill here?" but "is there room?" Four kinds of room
*(producer's practice, unverified: from teaching experience, not yet checked against a source)*:

- **Room in time.** Fills go where the voice is not. In a DAW, look at the vocal waveform: the flat gaps
  between its phrases are where a fill can go. A fill that starts before the singer finishes is cut back
  or moved.
- **Room in pitch.** A fill in the same range as the voice fights it. The ballad piano's answer sits above
  the voice, the bass walk-up below it.
- **Room in the stereo picture.** A guitar lick panned a little to one side of the centre (where the voice
  is) can be heard without covering a word.
- **Room in loudness.** Many producers bring a fill up with automation (a short rise on that track's
  fader) and keep the rest of the part low.

And the producer decides **who** answers: with three players able to fill, one is chosen for each gap,
and some gaps are left empty on purpose, so the fills that remain mean something. The band on this page
does the same: one player per gap, in turn.

## 9. Try it

- **Everyone:** play the ballad in section 2 with figures off and sing (or hum) a four-bar line over it.
  Then turn the fills on. Does the band answer you? Which answer suits the words?
- **Pianists:** switch the band's piano off in section 3 and play the answer and the sus yourself, slowly.
- **Bass players:** switch the bass off in section 4 and play the walk-up into each new chord.
- **Guitarists:** learn the riff in section 5 first (it repeats), then the lick (it answers).
- **Drummers:** play section 6 with the band's drums off. Fill only into bar 5.
- **Producers:** record a two-line vocal over the ballad in your DAW and place one fill in each gap. Try
  the same fill on two instruments and keep the one that is heard without covering the voice.
- **For your journal (Criterion B):** one sentence for each fill you tried: "I tried … in bar …; I kept /
  dropped it because …".
